PHSCS 587

Threshold, on-current and leakage

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how lowering threshold shifts an idealized logarithmic transfer curve

Threshold is both an electrostatic concept and a parameter extracted by a stated measurement rule. Different extraction methods can produce different numerical thresholds. Always report the biases and criterion used.

Lower threshold generally increases gate overdrive at a fixed supply, but also raises off-current. In weak inversion, a threshold reduction equal to one subthreshold swing raises modeled off-current tenfold. At the circuit level, a simple leakage estimate is Pstandby = NVDDIoff for N equally leaking off devices under the chosen state assumptions.

The ratio Ion/Ioff alone is not a complete device score: a threshold shift can change the ratio without providing the required drive at a permitted leakage level. Compare Ion at a specified Ioff, supply, geometry, load and temperature, or state the full design tradeoff.

Example

At S = 80 mV/decade, a 40 mV threshold reduction raises the idealized off-current by 10^(40/80) ≈ 3.16. For 10⁶ devices each leaking 2 nA at 0.8 V, the simplified standby estimate is 1.6 mW.

Sources and scope
  • PHSCS 587 reading: 6.3–6.3.3.1, threshold definitions and design
  • PHSCS 587, 6.3–6.3.3.1 recording 2: drive current, leakage, switching delay and threshold extraction.

Practice

1. Why is a larger Ion/Ioff ratio insufficient to select the better device for a fixed circuit?

Ask what absolute leakage, drive and supply the circuit permits.

The ratio hides absolute current levels and operating conditions. A circuit needs enough drive within its leakage, supply, capacitance and delay limits; devices must be compared at consistent constraints.
